In reality, the direction problem has two dimensions: first, the direction of test coverage is decided by humans (what to test and what not to test), and the Agent can only execute; second, once coverage reaches 90%, the risk of the uncovered 10% is amplified because teams become more confident in the parts that pass tests—and that 10% often contains the most critical edge cases. Traditional software engineering has abundant precedent for this paradox; it is not a theoretical concern.

Discovery cost isn't just "edge cases are hard to identify"; the deeper problem is that AI agents' training data comes from human engineers' historical code, so the distribution of edge cases they can conceive is isomorphic to human engineers'. If the edge cases in a test suite are themselves products of blind spots, 90% coverage may lock in a quality floor with systematic bias.
